hero_video.title: How the harvest moved
hero_video.aria: The 2025-26 harvest in Morelos advancing week by week on the map

how.heading: How it works
how.s1_title: Radar sees through clouds and smoke.
how.s1_text: The NISAR satellite, from NASA and India's space agency, passes over the cane fields every 12 days. It works day and night, even under cloudy skies.
how.s1_aria: Drawing: the satellite sends its signal through clouds and smoke down to the cane field, day and night, every 12 days.
how.s2_title: When cane is cut, the signal changes.
how.s2_text: A field with tall cane returns a different signal than a freshly cut one. The system detects that change.
how.s2_aria: Drawing: the same field before, with tall cane, and after, already cut.
how.s3_title: The map marks the date for each field.
how.s3_text: Every field shows the approximate day it was harvested, and you can watch the season move week by week.
how.s3_aria: Drawing: fields seen from above, each with its harvest date, such as Feb 12 and Mar 3.

who.heading: Who is it for?
who.mills_text: See how the harvest advances, week by week.

who.growers_text: Check on a public map which day each field was harvested.

who.aside: And it is low-cost: it uses free NASA imagery.

about.heading: Who's behind it
about.p1: I'm Juan Alberto Toledo Tello, a software developer with more than 9 years of experience, from Morelos, Mexico, and a graduate of Instituto Tecnológico de Zacatepec.
about.p2: I took part in Zafra Radar as a team of one, so I got to do a bit of everything: the satellite data analysis, the web app and its deployment. I built the web app in one weekend, with the help of AI coding agents and reviewing every step, during the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 at my old school, where 877 people took part in 170 teams.
about.p3: I enjoy taking an idea or a problem and turning it into something that works. If you have a project in mind, I'd be glad to talk.
